title: Is Parapsoriasis a variant of Mycosis fungoides?
summary:
Parapsoriasis is a rare disease. It is characterized by red to brown patches and plaques on the arms and legs. It is usually not very serious, but occasionally it has been described as developing into a skin lymphoma. The most common skin lymphoma, mycosis fungoides, has a very favorable prognosis in the early stages. In rare cases, however, it can progress to a tumor stage, which has a very aggressive course of disease. It is therefore debated whether parapsoriasis is a separate inflammatory skin disease, a precursor of MF or a variant of MF. The changes in the skin are often ambiguous, which makes it difficult to distinguish between the two diseases. Parapsoriasis is treated with glucocorticosteroids and UV therapy. Chloromethine gel can help with MF, but it is not approved for the treatment of parapsoriasis.
Because parapsoriasis and mycosis fungoides are similar, it is thought that parapsoriasis is a form of mycosis fungoides.
To verify this, we are comparing the skin of patients with parapsoriasis and early mycosis fungoides. We examine the cell building block RNA of the cells from skin tissue samples.

interventions.name:
Parapsoriasis (PP)

The examinations in the study are carried out ex vivo using archived skin biopsies.
Single cell transcriptomics and single nuclear transcriptomics as well as additional immunohistochemical staining are performed.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Patients with a confirmed diagnosis of early-stage cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides type)
- Patients with inflammatory skin diseases (eczema, psoriasis) and planned dermatosurgical intervention, where it is to be expected that non-lesional skin will also be excised
- Patients with clinically typical small-plaque parapsoriasis (SPP) and histologically appropriate findings as well as a documented course of at least 6 months
- Patients with clinically typical large-plaque parapsoriasis (LPP) and histologically appropriate findings and a documented course of at least 6 months
Exclusion criteria:
none
